What it connects to

## An agent that can only talk isn't much use.

Wysebee hands yours the three things it actually needs to finish a job — and nothing beyond what you hand over.

### Browser

Let it use the web like you do.

Point the agent at a page and it clicks, reads, scrolls and fills in forms — the same actions you would take, driven by the skill you gave it. The sites that have no API, the internal dashboard nobody will ever expose: still reachable.

- Pull a report nobody exposes an API for

- Fill the same form a hundred times

- Check a page and tell you what changed

### Containers

Give it a machine, not your machine.

Commands run inside the node's own Docker workspace — never on your host. The agent gets a real shell, a real filesystem and whatever runtime you pick, and it is sealed off from everything else you own.

- Run a script against real data

- Build, test, read the output

- Keep the work in one folder you can delete

### Databases

Answer questions in the data itself.

Connect the database you already run and the agent queries it directly — no export, no copy, no pipeline to maintain. What it can reach is exactly what you configured, and nothing else.

- Ask in plain English, get real rows

- Reconcile two systems that disagree

- Draft the migration, then show you it

## An agent with real hands needs real limits.

Letting something act on your behalf is the part that should make you nervous. Two things in Wysebee are built for exactly that worry — and both are on before the first step runs.

### You watch the work happen.

The agent does not disappear and come back with a result. Every action it takes is on screen as it takes it — the page it opened, the command it ran, the row it changed — so a wrong turn is something you catch in the moment, not something you discover afterwards.

- Each step surfaced as it happens, not summarised at the end

- Stop it mid-run; nothing is a black box you cannot interrupt

- The skill you wrote is the instruction set — no hidden prompt

### It gets a container, not your filesystem.

Shell commands never run on your host — they run inside the node's own Docker workspace, and the file tools can only reach that one folder. A poisoned web page can still try to steer the agent. It just lands somewhere that holds no secrets and can see one directory.

- cap_drop=ALL, no-new-privileges, an unprivileged uid, and memory/CPU/process ceilings

- An allow-listed environment built from scratch — never the one your shell has

- No credential key, no database route, and none of your source inside the container

- Paths resolve through symlinks before the containment check, so a link pointing out is caught like a ../ escape

One deliberate exception: the admin-only Local Command tool runs a fixed program on your host, because sometimes that is the point. Even then the arguments never reach a shell, and the environment is allow-listed.

Any provider

## Bring your own model. Or don't bring one at all.

Paste a key from whichever provider you already pay for — or point Wysebee at a model running on your own machine and skip the key entirely. Same agent, same tools, same screen; only the brain changes.

### Hosted, with a key

- OpenAI

- Anthropic

- Google Gemini

- Alibaba Cloud (Qwen)

- DeepSeek

- Mistral AI

- Sakana AI

Keys are encrypted on this machine. They can be replaced or removed, but are never shown again once saved — not in the UI, and not to the agent.

### Local, with no key

Ollama · LM Studio

Or any OpenAI-compatible server on your machine or your network. Point Wysebee at the URL, leave the key blank, and nothing leaves the machine — not the prompt, not the page the agent read, not the rows it queried.

Pick a model that supports tool calling — in Ollama, qwen3 or llama3.1 .

## It runs on your machine.

Wysebee Desktop turns your computer into a set of nodes — named bundles of tools you build by filling in a form — and gives your agent exactly those, and nothing else. The work happens where you can see it, on hardware you own.
